chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Ahmad ibn Idris (may God have mercy on him) narrated to us. He said: My father narrated to us from Ahmad ibn Abi Abdillah al-Barqi, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ubaydullah ibn Abdullah al-Dahqan, from Durust ibn Abi Mansur al-Wasiti, from Ibrahim ibn Abd al-Hamid, from Abu al-Hasan Musa ibn Ja'far, from his forefathers (peace be upon them), who said:

The Messenger of God (may God bless him and his family) entered the mosque, and there was a group of people gathered around a man. He asked: "What is this?" They said: "An allama (a great scholar)." He said: "And what is an allama?" They said: "He is the most knowledgeable of the people in the lineages of the Arabs and their battles, the days of the Jahiliyya, the poems, and the Arabic language." So the Prophet (may God bless him and his family) said: "That is a knowledge whose ignorance does not harm and whose familiarity does not benefit."

key_terms.أنساب العرب: Genealogies of the Arabs — a highly valued discipline in pre-Islamic and early Islamic Arabian society
key_terms.الجاهلية: Jahiliyya — the pre-Islamic era of ignorance
key_terms.علّامة: Allama — a superlative title meaning "very learned one," here used for a man versed in secular pre-Islamic knowledge

ai.seo_question: What did the Prophet Muhammad say about knowledge that does not benefit?
ai.summary: The Prophet Muhammad (SAWW), upon encountering a man celebrated as an "allama" for his expertise in pre-Islamic Arab genealogy, battles, and poetry, dismissed such knowledge as ultimately inconsequential. This teaching, delivered in the mosque in Medina, was directed at redirecting his community's attention from the scholarly traditions they had inherited from pre-Islamic culture toward knowledge that has genuine spiritual and moral benefit.
word_analysis: may God have mercy on him
